A Lecture in Ancient Mesopotamian History

The Sumerians

First Cities of Humankind · c. 5500 – 1750 BCE
  • The world's first known urban civilization, in southern Iraq.
  • Inventors of writing, the wheel, and the 60-minute hour.
  • Builders of Uruk, Ur, Eridu, and the great ziggurats.
  • A people whose ideas still shape daily life today.
Lecture Overview

What This Lecture Covers

Origins & Land

Who the Sumerians were, their homeland in the marshy south, and their mysterious language.

Cities & Uruk

The birth of the city, from Eridu and Uruk to Ur — the urban revolution.

Writing & Invention

Cuneiform, the wheel, base-60 math, law, and the tools that built civilization.

Gods, Kings & Legacy

Temples and ziggurats, kings and empires, and what Sumer gave the world.

Orientation

The Sumerian Age at a Glance

c.5500 BCE
First farmers settle the southern marshes in the Ubaid period.
c.3300 BCE
Writing is born at Uruk — the first true cities rise.
c.2334 BCE
Sargon of Akkad forges the world's first empire.
c.2004 BCE
Ur falls; Sumerian fades as a spoken tongue but lives on in scholarship.
Setting the Scene

The World of Sumer

Land of Two Rivers

The Tigris and Euphrates fed a hot, flat, fertile plain in what is now southern Iraq.

Marsh and Field

Reed marshes, date palms, and irrigated fields sustained the earliest cities.

Neighbors

Akkadians to the north, Elam to the east, and desert peoples all around.

A Crossroads

With little stone, timber, or metal, Sumer traded far to get what it lacked.

Why It Matters

Why the Sumerians Matter

They Invented Writing

Cuneiform, the earliest known writing system, began here around 3300 BCE.

They Built the First Cities

Uruk may have been the largest city on Earth in its day.

They Shaped Time

Our 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle descend from Sumerian math.

They Told the First Stories

The world's oldest literature, including Gilgamesh, was born in Sumer.

Part One

Origins & the Land of Sumer

  • The fertile plain between the Tigris and Euphrates.
  • The name 'Sumer' and the 'black-headed people'.
  • A language unrelated to any other on Earth.
  • The Ubaid beginnings and the mystery of their origin.
Introduction

Who Were the Sumerians?

City Builders

A people of southern Mesopotamia who created the world's first cities and states.

A Unique Tongue

They spoke Sumerian, a language isolate with no known relatives.

First Writers

They devised cuneiform, humanity's earliest writing, on clay tablets.

Deep Influence

Their inventions in law, math, and religion echoed across millennia.

The Land

The Land of Sumer

Between the Rivers

Sumer lay in the flood plain of the lower Tigris and Euphrates, in what is now southern Iraq — a hot, treeless land made rich by river silt.

  • Yearly floods left fertile mud but demanded irrigation and control.
  • Reed marshes near the Gulf teemed with fish, birds, and wildlife.
  • The land gave grain and clay in plenty — but no stone, metal, or timber.
The Name

Sumer and Kengir

'Sumer'

The name comes from the later Akkadians; it named the southern land and its people.

'Ki-en-gir'

The Sumerians called their own land Kengir, 'the country of the noble lords'.

'Emegir'

Their language they called Emegir, 'the native tongue'.

The South

Sumer meant the far south of Mesopotamia, below the city of Nippur.

Identity

The 'Black-Headed People'

Their Own Name

Sumerians called themselves the 'black-headed people' (sag-gig-ga).

A Proud Identity

The phrase set them apart as a distinct people with their own gods and kings.

Language, Not Race

'Sumerian' today means a language and culture, not a single ethnic group.

A Mixed World

From early on, Sumerians lived beside Semitic-speaking Akkadians and others.

The Language

The Sumerian Language

A Language Isolate

Sumerian is unrelated to Semitic, Indo-European, or any known family.

Written for Millennia

Though it died as a spoken tongue, it was written for over 2,000 years.

Agglutinative

It built words by stacking prefixes and suffixes onto roots.

Recovered by Scholars

Modern scholars deciphered it through bilingual Akkadian texts.

A Mystery

Where Did They Come From?

An Open Question

Whether Sumerians were natives of the plain or migrants is still debated.

The Local View

Many scholars see them as the local heirs of the Ubaid marsh villagers.

The Migration View

Others once proposed arrival from the east or a highland homeland.

No Clear Answer

Their true origin remains one of archaeology's open puzzles.

Beginnings

The Ubaid Foundations

Long before cities, farming villages spread across the southern plain.

First Farmers

From c. 5500 BCE, Ubaid villagers farmed grain and herded animals.

Early Shrines

Small mud-brick temples at Eridu grew, layer on layer, over centuries.

Mastering Water

Simple canals let farmers tame the rivers and expand their fields.

Toward Towns

Some villages swelled into towns — the seeds of the coming cities.

Daily Life

Life in the Marshes

A Watery World

The southern marshes shaped early Sumerian life, offering reeds, fish, and shelter along the water's edge.

  • Reed was cut for houses, boats, mats, and even writing tools.
  • Fish and waterfowl enriched a diet built on barley and dates.
  • The same marsh way of life still survives among Iraq's Marsh Arabs today.
The First City

Eridu: Where It Began

Eridu
In Sumerian tradition the oldest city of all — home of the wisdom-god Enki, and one of the first places kingship was said to descend from heaven.

A Sacred Site

Its temple was rebuilt on the same spot for thousands of years.

God of Water

Eridu honored Enki, lord of fresh water and wisdom.

First of Cities

The Sumerian King List names Eridu as the first seat of kingship.

Debate

Sumerians and Their Neighbors

Semitic Neighbors

Akkadian-speakers lived among and around the Sumerians from early times.

Blending Cultures

Sumerian and Akkadian ideas, gods, and words mixed for centuries.

Two Tongues

For ages the region was bilingual, in Sumerian and Akkadian.

Shared Kingship

Later kings often ruled 'Sumer and Akkad' together as one realm.

Summary

Origins: Key Takeaways

People of the Rivers

Southerners of the Tigris–Euphrates plain, rooted in the Ubaid past.

Alone in Language

Speakers of a unique isolate tongue, known now only through their texts.

Makers of Cities

The first people known to gather in true cities and states.

World Shapers

Founders of traditions in writing, faith, and law that outlived them.

Part Two

The Rise of Cities

  • The urban revolution of the Uruk period.
  • Eridu, Uruk, Ur, and the great city-states.
  • Temples, walls, and the world's first crowds.
  • How the city reshaped human life forever.
The Great Change

The Urban Revolution

A New Way to Live

Around 4000–3100 BCE, villages in Sumer grew into true cities.

Crowds of Strangers

For the first time, thousands lived together beyond kin and village.

Temple at the Heart

Great temples organized labor, storage, and worship.

New Roles

Priests, scribes, craftsmen, and rulers emerged as specialists.

The First Metropolis

Uruk: The First Great City

Home of Gilgamesh

Uruk was the beating heart of early Sumer — perhaps the largest city on Earth around 3100 BCE, and the setting of the world's oldest epic.

  • Its brick walls, remembered in legend, were credited to King Gilgamesh.
  • Vast temple complexes honored the sky-god An and the goddess Inanna.
  • Writing itself first appears in the temple archives of Uruk.
A City of Thousands

The Scale of Uruk

40,000
A rough estimate of Uruk's population at its height — a staggering crowd for its age, ringed by walls that ran for kilometers around the city.

A Human Sea

Tens of thousands lived where villages once held dozens.

Mighty Walls

Legend credited its great walls to the hero-king Gilgamesh.

Twin Temples

The precincts of Eanna and Kullaba anchored the city.

The Cities

The Great City-States of Sumer

Eridu

The oldest city, sacred to Enki, god of wisdom and fresh water.

Uruk

The largest early city, home of Inanna, An, and Gilgamesh.

Ur

A rich southern port, sacred to the moon-god Nanna.

Nippur

The holy city of Enlil — never a capital, but Sumer's spiritual center.

More Cities

A Land of Rival Cities

Lagash & Girsu

A powerful state whose god was the warrior Ningirsu.

Kish

A northern city whose kings claimed leadership over Sumer.

Umma

Lagash's bitter rival in a long war over farmland.

Larsa & Others

Adab, Shuruppak, Bad-tibira, and more dotted the plain.

A Great City

Ur: The Southern Metropolis

Jewel of the South

Ur was among Sumer's richest cities — a bustling river port sacred to the moon-god Nanna, and later the seat of a great empire.

  • Its harbors linked Sumer to the Gulf and lands far beyond.
  • Its royal tombs held some of the ancient world's finest treasures.
  • Under Ur-Nammu it became the capital of all Sumer.
A Holy City

Nippur: Heart of the Gods

Nippur held a place like no other — sacred to Enlil, chief of the gods, and honored by every Sumerian city.

City of Enlil

Its great temple, the Ekur, was the holiest in all Sumer.

Kingmaker

No king felt secure until Nippur's priests blessed his rule.

A Library in Clay

Its 'Tablet Hill' yielded much of surviving Sumerian literature.

Never a Capital

Sacred and neutral, it stood above the quarrels of kings.

City Plan

Inside a Sumerian City

The Temple Core

A towering temple and its estate stood at the city's heart.

Walls and Gates

Thick mud-brick walls ringed the city against raiders and rivals.

Crowded Lanes

Flat-roofed brick houses lined narrow, winding streets.

Canals and Quays

Waterways carried goods to harbors within and beyond the walls.

Building Material

A World of Mud-Brick

Clay Into Cities

Lacking stone and timber, Sumerians built everything from the mud beneath their feet, shaped into sun-dried and kiln-fired brick.

  • Reeds and bitumen strengthened walls, roofs, and foundations.
  • Whole cities rose, decayed, and were rebuilt on their own rubble.
  • Over ages these mounds grew into the 'tells' that mark Iraq today.
The Temple Estate

The Temple as Institution

The great temple was far more than a house of worship.

House of the God

Each city was seen as the earthly estate of its patron deity.

Vast Landholder

Temples owned fields, herds, and workshops across the land.

Economic Engine

They stored grain, employed labor, and redistributed goods.

Birth of Records

Tracking all this wealth drove the invention of writing.

Society

The People of the City

Rulers & Priests

Kings (lugal) and city-governors (ensi) led with the priesthood.

Scribes

A trained scribal class kept records and ran the bureaucracy.

Craftsmen

Potters, smiths, weavers, and builders filled busy workshops.

Farmers & Laborers

Most people worked the fields that fed the whole city.

Trade

Reaching Across the World

Long-Distance Trade

Sumer traded grain and cloth for metal, stone, and timber.

Precious Imports

Lapis lazuli came from Afghanistan, copper from Oman and beyond.

River and Sea

Boats carried cargo down the rivers and across the Gulf.

Seals of Trust

Cylinder seals marked ownership and sealed deals across distances.

A Distant Land

Dilmun and the Sea Trade

Gateway to the Gulf

Sumerian texts speak of Dilmun — modern Bahrain — as a sacred, paradise-like land and a vital hub of Gulf trade.

  • Through Dilmun flowed copper, pearls, and exotic goods.
  • Myth cast Dilmun as a pure land where the gods dwelt.
  • The sea trade linked Sumer to distant Magan and Meluhha.
Water

Taming the Rivers

Life and Danger

The rivers gave life but flooded fiercely and shifted their beds.

Canals

Networks of canals spread water across the thirsty fields.

Shared Labor

Digging and cleaning canals demanded organized communal work.

Cause of War

Rights to water and land sparked wars between rival cities.

Summary

The City: Key Takeaways

Birthplace of Cities

Sumer gave the world its first true urban centers.

Temple-Centered

Great temples organized faith, labor, and wealth.

New Society

Kings, priests, scribes, and craftsmen — a complex order was born.

Connected World

Trade tied resource-poor Sumer to lands far away.

Part Three

Writing & Invention

  • Cuneiform: humanity's first writing.
  • The wheel, the plow, and the sail.
  • Base-60 math and the measure of time.
  • Schools, law, and the tools of civilization.
The Great Invention

The Birth of Writing

From Tokens to Tablets

Writing began not with poetry but with accounting — the need to record grain, sheep, and goods in the temple storehouses of Uruk.

  • Early scribes pressed pictures and numbers into wet clay tablets.
  • Over time pictures became abstract wedge-shaped signs.
  • This is the oldest writing system known, from around 3300 BCE.
Cuneiform

How Cuneiform Worked

Wedges in Clay

A reed stylus pressed wedge-shaped marks into soft clay.

Signs for Sounds

Signs stood for whole words and, later, for syllables and sounds.

A Shared Script

The same script was adapted to write Akkadian and many other tongues.

Baked to Last

Fired or dried clay tablets survived for thousands of years.

Deep Time

Older Than the Pyramids

3300
The approximate year BCE when writing first appears in Sumer — centuries before Egypt's pyramids, making cuneiform the oldest known script on Earth.

First Script

The earliest writing yet found anywhere in the world.

Before the Pyramids

Writing predates Giza's great pyramids by centuries.

A Long Life

Cuneiform stayed in use for over three thousand years.

The Scribe

Scribes and Schools

Writing created a powerful new profession — and the world's first schools.

The Scribe

Trained scribes kept accounts, letters, contracts, and law.

The Edubba

The 'tablet house' was the Sumerian school where scribes learned.

Hard Study

Students copied signs endlessly and faced strict discipline.

A Path to Power

Literacy opened doors to temple, palace, and high office.

The Wheel

The Wheel

Potter's Wheel

The wheel first spun as a tool for shaping pottery.

Wheeled Vehicles

Carts and wagons soon rolled on solid wooden wheels.

War and Work

Wheeled wagons carried goods, people, and warriors.

World-Changer

Few inventions reshaped human life as deeply as the wheel.

The Plow

Farming Inventions

The Seed Plow

A plow that cut a furrow and dropped seed in one motion.

Irrigation

Canals and dikes turned dry plain into rich farmland.

Surplus

Efficient farming fed cities and freed people for other work.

Farmer's Almanac

A Sumerian text gave step-by-step advice on growing barley.

The Measure of Time

Base-60 and the Hour

60
The Sumerian sexagesimal system — counting in sixties — still rules our clocks and maps: 60 seconds, 60 minutes, and the 360 degrees of a circle.

Hours & Minutes

Our 60-minute hour descends directly from Sumerian math.

The Circle

The 360-degree circle comes from their base-60 counting.

Easy Fractions

Sixty divides neatly, making trade and measurement simple.

Mathematics

Sumerian Mathematics

Base-60

A sexagesimal system for counting, trade, and measurement.

Geometry

Scribes measured fields, canals, and stores of grain.

Number Tables

Clay tablets held multiplication and reciprocal tables.

Legacy in Time

Their math still ticks in every clock and compass today.

More Inventions

Tools That Built a World

The Sail

Boats caught the wind to move goods along river and sea.

Arch & Vault

Builders spanned space with the true arch and vault in brick.

Cylinder Seals

Rolled seals signed documents and secured property.

Metalworking

Smiths cast copper and bronze into tools and weapons.

Law

The First Law Codes

Justice in Writing

Sumer produced the earliest known written laws, setting fines and penalties to bring order and fairness to city life.

  • The Code of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BCE) is the oldest surviving law code.
  • It predates the famous laws of Hammurabi by three centuries.
  • Many laws set precise silver fines rather than harsh bodily revenge.
Measurement

Weights, Measures, and Trade

Standard Weights

Fixed weights let merchants trade fairly across cities.

Silver as Money

Weighed silver served as a common measure of value.

Written Contracts

Deals, loans, and sales were recorded on sealed tablets.

Trust at a Distance

Standards and seals made long-distance trade possible.

Knowledge

Recording the World

Word Lists

Scribes compiled long lists of words, gods, places, and things.

Watching the Sky

Careful sky-watching laid foundations for later astronomy.

Practical Science

Texts gathered knowledge of farming, medicine, and craft.

The Calendar

A lunar calendar of twelve months ordered the working year.

Everyday Life

Daily Life in Sumer

Bread and Beer

Barley fed the people as bread and as thick, nourishing beer.

Family and Home

Families lived in mud-brick homes around shared courtyards.

Music and Games

Lyres, board games, and festivals brightened city life.

Law and Order

Contracts and courts governed marriage, property, and trade.

An Art Form

The Cylinder Seal

A Signature in Stone

A carved stone cylinder rolled a signature scene into wet clay.

Tiny Masterpieces

Seals bore gods, heroes, animals, and rituals in miniature.

Proof and Property

They sealed jars, doors, and documents against tampering.

A Personal Mark

Each seal was unique to its owner — an identity carved in stone.

Healing

Medicine and Healing

Oldest Prescriptions

A Sumerian tablet of remedies is the earliest known medical text.

Herbal Cures

Healers drew on plants, minerals, and animal products.

Magic and Medicine

Illness was met with both remedies and ritual against demons.

Careful Observers

Scribes recorded symptoms, treatments, and their outcomes.

Summary

Invention: Key Takeaways

The First Writers

Cuneiform, the oldest script, began in Sumer's temples.

Masters of Time

Base-60 math still measures our hours and circles.

Great Inventors

The wheel, plow, sail, and arch transformed human life.

Rule of Law

The earliest written laws sought order and justice.

Part Four

Gods, Temples & Ziggurats

  • A crowded pantheon of powerful gods.
  • An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna, and Nanna.
  • The ziggurat: a mountain of brick for the gods.
  • Myths, priests, and the fear of the afterlife.
Belief

The Sumerian Worldview

Gods Everywhere

Gods ruled every force of nature — sky, storm, water, and grain.

Servants of the Gods

Humans were made, myth said, to serve and feed the gods.

Divine Cities

Each city belonged to a god who dwelt in its great temple.

Order and Fate

The gods set the 'me' — the divine decrees that ordered the world.

The Great Gods

The Chief Gods of Sumer

An

The remote sky-god and father of the gods, honored at Uruk.

Enlil

Lord of wind and storm, the ruling power, enthroned at Nippur.

Enki

God of fresh water, wisdom, and craft, dwelling at Eridu.

Ninhursag

The great mother-goddess of earth, birth, and life.

More Gods

Sun, Moon, and Star

Nanna (Sin)

The moon-god, lord of Ur, who measured out the months.

Utu (Shamash)

The sun-god, all-seeing lord of justice and truth.

Inanna (Ishtar)

Goddess of love and war, and the planet Venus.

Ereshkigal

Dread queen of the underworld, the land of no return.

The Goddess

Inanna, Queen of Heaven

Love and War

Inanna of Uruk was the most vivid of Sumer's deities — goddess of love, fertility, and war, and the bright planet Venus in the sky.

  • Her myths tell of passion, ambition, and daring journeys.
  • The 'Descent of Inanna' follows her into the underworld and back.
  • As Ishtar she became one of the most worshipped goddesses of the East.
The Temple

The House of the God

Where Heaven Met Earth

Every Sumerian city rose around the house of its god — a temple served day and night, as if the deity truly lived within.

  • Priests washed, clothed, and 'fed' the god's statue with offerings.
  • The temple estate employed and fed much of the city.
  • Festivals and processions bound the whole community to its god.
Sacred Mountain

The Ziggurat

A Stairway to the Gods

The ziggurat was Sumer's grandest creation in brick — a vast stepped platform raising the god's shrine toward the heavens.

  • Solid mud-brick cores were faced with tougher fired brick.
  • A shrine at the summit crowned the towering terraces.
  • The ziggurat stood as the visible link between the city and its god.
The Great Ziggurat

The Ziggurat of Ur

Ur
The best-preserved ziggurat in the world still rises near Nasiriyah in southern Iraq — built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE for the moon-god Nanna.

Still Standing

Its massive base survives after four thousand years.

For the Moon-God

Raised to honor Nanna, divine lord of the city of Ur.

Ur-Nammu's Work

Built by the founder of Ur's last great dynasty.

Priesthood

Priests and Worship

Servants of the God

Priests tended the deity's statue and ran the temple estate.

Priest and King

Rulers led key rites; some priestesses held great power.

Offerings

Grain, beer, meat, and incense were offered daily to the gods.

Reading Signs

Priests sought the gods' will in omens and the sky.

Myths

The Stories They Told

A Great Flood

A Sumerian flood myth tells of a hero who survived the deluge.

Inanna's Descent

The goddess braves the underworld and bargains her way back.

Enki and Creation

Tales of Enki explain the ordering of the world and its waters.

The King List

A famous text blends myth and history from before the flood.

The Afterlife

Death and the Underworld

The Great Below

The dead went to Kur, a dim, dusty land of no return.

A Grim Fate

Sumerians pictured a bleak afterlife, not a paradise.

Grave Goods

The dead were buried with food, tools, and treasures.

Royal Tombs

Ur's royal graves held stunning riches — and human attendants.

A Stunning Find

The Royal Tombs of Ur

Buried Treasure

Excavation uncovered graves rich with gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.

Queen Puabi

One tomb held a queen adorned in a spectacular golden headdress.

The Great Lyres

Exquisite bull-headed lyres lay among the royal burials.

The Death Pits

Attendants were laid to rest beside their royal masters.

A Famous Woman

Enheduanna, the First Author

The First Named Poet

Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon-god at Ur, is the earliest author in history known by name — a princess who signed her own hymns.

  • She was a daughter of Sargon of Akkad, placed to rule Ur's great temple.
  • Her passionate hymns to Inanna survive on clay tablets.
  • She wrote in the first person, centuries before any other named author.
Ritual

Festivals and the Sacred Year

The New Year

Great festivals marked the turning of the Sumerian year.

Sacred Rites

Kings performed rituals to renew the land's fertility and order.

Processions

Gods' statues traveled by boat and road between temple cities.

Reading the Heavens

Priests watched moon and stars to time the sacred calendar.

Sacred Places

Holy Cities of Sumer

Nippur

Enlil's city, the spiritual heart that no king could ignore.

Eridu

Enki's ancient shrine, revered as the first of all cities.

Ur

Nanna's city, crowned by its towering ziggurat.

Uruk

Home of An and Inanna, and of the first great temples.

Summary

Religion: Key Takeaways

Gods in Every City

Each city lived to serve its own divine lord.

Mountains of Brick

Ziggurats raised the gods above the flat plain.

The First Myths

Sumer's stories of gods, floods, and heroes shaped later faiths.

A Named Voice

Enheduanna became history's first author known by name.

Part Five

Kings, City-States & Empire

  • The Early Dynastic age of warring cities.
  • Gilgamesh, Eannatum, and the reformer Urukagina.
  • Sargon of Akkad and the first empire.
  • Gudea, Ur-Nammu, and the Sumerian Renaissance.
Power

How Sumer Was Ruled

The Lugal

The 'big man', or king, led in war and grand building.

The Ensi

A city-governor ruled as steward of the city's god.

Assembly

Elders and citizens once shared in a city's decisions.

Divine Mandate

Kingship, the King List says, 'descended from heaven'.

The King List

The Sumerian King List

A Grand Chronicle

It lists the cities and kings said to have ruled Sumer in turn.

Before the Flood

Its first kings reign for fantastical thousands of years.

Passing the Crown

Kingship moves from city to city as fortunes rise and fall.

Myth and History

It mixes legend with real rulers and real cities.

The Hero-King

Gilgamesh of Uruk

King and Legend

Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk in the Early Dynastic age, became the hero of the world's oldest great epic — a tale of friendship, loss, and the search for eternal life.

  • Legend credited him with Uruk's mighty walls.
  • His epic wrestles with mortality and the meaning of a life.
  • It contains a famous flood story echoed in later traditions.
Early Dynastic

An Age of Rival Cities

City Against City

From c. 2900 BCE, independent cities fought for land and water.

Lagash and Umma

A bitter, generations-long border war divided these neighbors.

Shifting Power

No single city held lasting mastery over the whole land.

Walls and Warriors

Warfare drove strong walls, armies, and ambitious kings.

A Long Feud

The War of Lagash and Umma

A Fight for Water

The two cities clashed for generations over fertile border land.

An Early Treaty

A border was fixed, marked by boundary stones and oaths to the gods.

Broken Peace

Time and again the truce failed and the fighting resumed.

Recorded in Stone

Their struggle is among history's earliest documented wars.

War in Stone

Eannatum and the Stele of the Vultures

The Oldest War Record

Eannatum of Lagash left the Stele of the Vultures — the earliest known monument to record a real historical battle, his victory over rival Umma.

  • Its carvings show massed soldiers in helmets and locked shields.
  • Vultures wheel over the enemy dead, giving the stele its name.
  • It is among the first works to blend history, art, and propaganda.
A Reformer

Urukagina's Reforms

The First Reformer

Urukagina of Lagash (c. 2350 BCE) issued what many call history's first recorded reforms, curbing abuses by officials and protecting the weak.

  • He claimed to defend widows and orphans from the powerful.
  • He cut greedy fees and reined in overbearing officials.
  • His texts are an early cry for social justice, written in clay.
Unification

The First Conqueror-Kings

Lugalzagesi

The king of Umma briefly united much of Sumer by force.

One Ruler

For a moment, many cities bowed to a single overlord.

Fragile Power

Such conquests were swift, but rarely outlived their maker.

A Sign of Things

They hinted at the great empire soon to come from the north.

The First Empire

Sargon of Akkad

Founder of Empire

Around 2334 BCE, Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and forged the world's first true empire, ruling 'Sumer and Akkad' together.

  • He rose, legend says, from humble birth to universal king.
  • His Akkadian language spread widely across Mesopotamia.
  • His dynasty ruled for over a century before it fell.
The Akkadians

The Akkadian Century

Sargon's Line

Sargon, his sons, and grandson Naram-Sin ruled a vast realm.

Naram-Sin

A mighty king who called himself a god and 'king of the four quarters'.

Akkadian Rises

Semitic Akkadian grew into the language of power and trade.

Collapse

Revolt, and raids by the Gutians, brought the empire down.

Interlude

The Gutian Interlude

Highland Raiders

The Gutians, a people from the Zagros, overran the land.

A Dark Time

Later scribes remembered their rule as chaotic and harsh.

Cities Endure

Some southern cities kept their independence and prospered.

Ripe for Revival

Their fall opened the way for a Sumerian comeback.

The Pious Ruler

Gudea of Lagash

The Devout Builder

As Gutian power waned, Gudea of Lagash ruled a peaceful, prosperous city and left dozens of serene statues of himself in prayer.

  • He rebuilt the great temple of the god Ningirsu.
  • His inscriptions boast of trade for cedar, stone, and metal.
  • His polished diorite statues are masterpieces of Sumerian art.
The Renaissance

The Third Dynasty of Ur

A Sumerian Revival

Around 2112 BCE, Ur-Nammu founded the Third Dynasty of Ur, ushering in a golden 'Sumerian Renaissance' of order, building, and learning.

  • It reunited the south under a single, well-run government.
  • Sumerian flourished again as the language of court and temple.
  • It gave us the great ziggurat of Ur and the oldest law code.
Ur-Nammu

Ur-Nammu, Founder of Ur III

The Founder

Ur-Nammu reunited Sumer and founded its last great dynasty.

The Great Ziggurat

He raised the towering ziggurat of Ur for the moon-god.

The Law Code

His name marks the oldest surviving code of written law.

Roads and Order

He rebuilt canals, roads, and temples across the land.

The Great King

Shulgi of Ur

The Model King

Ur-Nammu's son Shulgi reigned nearly half a century, perfecting the empire's administration and even having himself worshipped as a god.

  • He built a vast bureaucracy that recorded everything in clay.
  • He reformed weights, measures, and the calendar across the realm.
  • He founded schools and praised himself as scholar, athlete, and king.
Ur III State

The Empire of Ur

A Clay Bureaucracy

Tens of thousands of tablets recorded the empire's every transaction.

Standardized Rule

Uniform weights, taxes, and calendars bound the provinces.

Frontier Walls

Kings built walls to hold back the Amorites and other peoples.

Faith Renewed

Temples and ziggurats rose across the reunited land.

Summary

Kings & Empire: Key Takeaways

Warring Cities

Sumer began as a patchwork of proud, rival city-states.

The First Empire

Sargon of Akkad first bound the whole land under one crown.

The Ur Revival

The Third Dynasty of Ur restored a brilliant Sumerian age.

Order in Clay

Law, records, and administration reached new heights.

Decline, Legacy & Rediscovery

Warning Signs

The Fall of Ur

Failing Fields

Salt built up in over-irrigated soil, weakening the harvests.

Amorite Pressure

Semitic Amorite peoples pressed in from the western deserts.

Elam Strikes

From the east, Elam invaded and struck at the heart of Ur.

The City Falls

Around 2004 BCE, Ur was sacked and its last king carried off.

A Lament

The Lament for Ur

A City Mourned

The fall of Ur was mourned in a haunting poem — the 'Lament for the Destruction of Ur' — one of the most moving works of Sumerian literature.

  • It pictures the moon-god's city emptied and its people scattered.
  • The gods themselves are said to abandon the ruined city.
  • Such laments became a lasting form in Mesopotamian poetry.
The End of an Era

The End of Sumerian Rule

No More Sumerian Kings

After Ur III, power passed to Amorite and other dynasties.

Isin and Larsa

Rival cities carried the old traditions into a new age.

A Dying Tongue

Sumerian faded from daily speech by around 2000 BCE.

But Not Forgotten

Its writing and learning lived on under new rulers.

A Living Language

Sumerian as a Sacred Tongue

The 'Latin' of Mesopotamia

Though it died as a spoken language, Sumerian survived for two thousand more years as the sacred, scholarly language of Mesopotamia.

  • Babylonian and Assyrian scribes still learned it in school.
  • Priests chanted Sumerian hymns long after the last native speaker.
  • Bilingual tablets preserved it — and later let scholars decipher it.
A Long Afterlife

Written for Two Millennia

2,000
The span in years that Sumerian endured as a written language of religion and scholarship, long after it vanished from the streets — a cultural afterlife few tongues can match.

Beyond Speech

It outlived its speakers by some two thousand years.

Sacred Script

Priests and scholars kept it alive in temple and school.

Key to the Past

Its survival let modern scholars recover Sumer's voice.

Legacy

What Sumer Gave the World

Writing

Cuneiform seeded the very idea of recording language.

Time & the Circle

The 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle are Sumerian.

Law & the City

The first codes, cities, and bureaucracies began here.

Literature

The world's oldest stories and hymns were composed in Sumer.

The Great Epic

The Epic of Gilgamesh

Humanity's Oldest Epic

Rooted in Sumerian tales of King Gilgamesh, the great epic is the oldest surviving masterpiece of world literature — a meditation on friendship and death.

  • It follows the hero's grief and his hopeless quest for eternal life.
  • Its flood story strikingly parallels later biblical accounts.
  • It still speaks to readers four thousand years later.
Influence

Echoes Down the Ages

Later Empires

Babylon and Assyria built directly on Sumerian foundations.

Shared Stories

Flood and creation tales echoed across the ancient Near East.

Everyday Life

We still keep Sumerian time whenever we read a clock.

Ideas of Justice

Their written law began a tradition that shapes us still.

Recovery

Rediscovering Sumer

A Lost World Found

For thousands of years Sumer was utterly forgotten. Only in the 1800s did scholars, digging into Iraq's mounds, recover a civilization no one remembered.

  • Cuneiform was deciphered, and a wholly unknown language emerged.
  • In 1872 a flood tablet stunned the world with its biblical echoes.
  • Excavations slowly revealed Sumer as the source of much that followed.
Archaeology

Unearthing the Cities

Digging the Tells

Archaeologists opened the great mounds of the southern plain.

The Royal Tombs of Ur

Woolley's 1920s dig at Ur revealed dazzling royal treasure.

Nippur's Tablets

Tens of thousands of tablets recovered Sumer's literature.

Restoring Ur

The ziggurat of Ur was partly restored and still stands.

Sumer Today

The Land of Sumer in Iraq

Ur

The great ziggurat rises near Nasiriyah in the south.

Uruk

The vast ruins of Warka mark the first great city.

Eridu

The mound of the oldest city sits amid the desert south.

Girsu & Nippur

Ancient Lagash and holy Nippur still yield their secrets.

World Heritage

Sumer as World Heritage

A Heritage for the World

In 2016, UNESCO honored the Ahwar of southern Iraq — the marshes and the ancient cities of Uruk, Ur, and Eridu — as a World Heritage site.

  • The listing joins living marshes with the world's first cities.
  • It recognizes Sumer as a cradle of urban civilization.
  • These sites are a source of deep pride for modern Iraq.
Reflection

Lessons from Sumer

The Power of Ideas

Writing and the city, born here, reshaped all human history.

Fragile Foundations

Even great civilizations depend on soil, water, and care.

Memory Endures

What is written down can outlive empires by millennia.

A Human First

Sumer reminds us how much of our world began in one place.

Summary

The Sumerians: In Brief

First Cities

They built the world's earliest cities on the southern plain.

First Writing

They invented cuneiform, the root of the written word.

First to Measure Time

Their base-60 math still orders our hours and circles.

First Stories

They composed humanity's oldest literature and law.

Conclusion
